claims.text: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical performance at 1600 °C.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has been predicted using first-principles calculations.
Adding approximately 3–5 at% Ti to equal-atomic NbMoTaW will improve its room-temperature ductility.
The Ti addition will promote nanoscale local ordering or controlled secondary-phase formation at grain boundaries.
Ti-induced local ordering or grain-boundary secondary phases will lower the barrier for room-temperature dislocation motion.
Ti-induced structural modifications will facilitate a transformation-induced plasticity response or activate additional slip systems.
Facilitating transformation-induced plasticity or additional slip systems will increase low-temperature dislocation mobility and ductility.
The 3–5 at% Ti addition will retain the dominant BCC phase at high temperature.
The Ti-modified alloy will maintain the baseline alloy's high strength and structural integrity at 1600 °C.
Irradiation tolerance in the Ti-modified alloy will remain governed by chemical homogeneity and atomic-scale disorder.
The Ti-modified alloy will exhibit irradiation-damage resistance comparable to untreated NbMoTaW.
The beneficial effect is restricted to a narrow Ti concentration range of approximately 3–5 at%.
Ti concentrations above the proposed range may produce brittle intermetallic phases.
Brittle intermetallic phases produced at higher Ti concentrations may compromise high-temperature and irradiation performance.
Direct experimental evidence linking minor Ti additions to improved room-temperature ductility without detrimental side effects is currently lacking.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field characterizes irradiation resistance as being based on first-principles predictions, whereas the baseline calls irradiation resistance 'documented,' which suggests an established baseline property rather than a primarily computational proposal.
